title: What Are Pasteurized Eggs and How Are They Different From Regular Eggs?

seo.title: Pasteurized Eggs: What They Are and When to Use Them
seo.meta_description: Pasteurization uses a controlled treatment to destroy Salmonella without necessarily turning the egg into a cooked egg. It can apply to shell eggs or egg products.
seo.search_intent: Understand what egg pasteurization means, how it changes microbiological risk, and when pasteurized eggs are useful.

excerpt: A pasteurized egg has received a validated treatment designed to destroy viable Salmonella. It can still look raw and behave similarly in recipes, but it adds a safety barrier for dishes that do not fully cook the egg.
content_html:
Pasteurizing an egg means applying a controlled treatment designed to destroy pathogens, especially Salmonella, without necessarily turning the product into a fully cooked egg. Shoppers may encounter pasteurized eggs still in the shell as well as liquid, frozen, or dried egg products that receive validated safety treatments.

USDA explains that shell eggs can be commercially pasteurized using processes accepted for Salmonella destruction. Doing this reliably at home is difficult because the margin between enough heat for pasteurization and enough heat to start coagulating white or yolk is narrow.

Pasteurization addresses a risk that can exist inside the egg

Salmonella contamination is not limited to the outside of the shell. An egg can become contaminated during formation before the shell is complete. Washing the exterior therefore does not replace a validated treatment of the contents.

Pasteurization is built around a time-and-temperature combination capable of reducing the target microorganism. In liquid egg products, industrial equipment can control that treatment very precisely before packaging.

Pasteurized does not mean sterile or shelf-stable forever

The treatment reduces important pathogens, but the product can still be contaminated after processing through poor handling. Refrigeration, dates, and manufacturer directions still matter. USDA continues to recommend hygienic handling for pasteurized egg products.

Pasteurization is also different from ordinary cooking. An in-shell pasteurized egg can still have a liquid white and yolk and work in many recipes much like a conventional egg.

They are especially useful when a recipe remains raw or lightly cooked

Homemade mayonnaise, some sauces, tiramisu, ice cream, and similar dishes may use egg without reaching normal cooking temperatures. In those cases, a pasteurized product reduces Salmonella risk compared with an ordinary raw shell egg.

USDA recommends pasteurized egg products for recipes traditionally made with raw egg. That choice is particularly relevant for people at higher risk of severe foodborne illness.

Good hygiene still matters after pasteurization

Once a liquid carton is opened, hands, utensils, and surfaces can introduce new contamination. The product should not sit at room temperature for extended periods. Follow storage directions and keep it away from cross-contamination with raw foods.

The practical rule: think of pasteurization as an added microbiological safety barrier, not permission to ignore storage and hygiene. When a recipe will not thoroughly cook the egg, a pasteurized product is the more controlled choice.

When reading an egg carton, separate three ideas: production system, size, and quality or freshness. None of those signals should replace the others. A color, code, or letter tells you about one specific characteristic; it does not by itself summarize nutrition, welfare, safety, or cooking performance.

faq.question: Is a pasteurized egg already cooked?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. The process is designed to destroy pathogens without fully coagulating the egg.

faq.question: Can I pasteurize eggs at home?
faq.answer: USDA says reliable home pasteurization is difficult without beginning to cook the egg.

faq.question: When are pasteurized eggs most useful?
faq.answer: For dishes containing raw or lightly cooked egg, such as certain sauces, mayonnaise, and desserts.
